The site from which the object comes has to be a primary parameter of the classification. Now that seals and inscriptions coming from one and the same site will be distributed in several volumes, a flexible new numbering system is required which will both allow additions at will and make it easy to place the object in its proper context.71 The Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions employs a separate consecutive numbering for each site, prefixed by a letter code which is more easily remembered than a numerical code. The major sites have a short, one-letter code. These sites are, moreover, arranged in each volume according to the total number of seals and inscriptions found at them, in the descending order. The sites which are "smaller" (in respect to the number of seals and inscriptions found at them) have a two-, three- or four-lettered code corresponding to their standard archaeological abbreviations and they are arranged in alphabetical order for easy reference. (See the table of contents.) The letter prefix for the site is followed by a dash and the number of the object assigned to it by its place within the classification sequence. Thus the objects from Mohenjo-daro in this first volume are numbered M-1 to M-620, and they are followed by the objects from Harappa starting with H-1. The objects from Mohenjo-daro in the second volume will start with M-621. Any number of additions can be made. The Chalcolithic period in the Ahar-Banas is generally divided into three phases based on archaeological materials and radiocarbon dates from various sites. The best evidence for the early periods is preserved at Balathal (Mishra 2005), while the layers excavated at Gilund (Shinde et al. 2014) and Ahar (Sankalia et al. 1969) seem to fall into the middle and later periods. Newly published radiocarbon dates from Pachamta (Raczek et al. 2019) seem to confirm the chronological horizon of the later part of the Ahar-Banas Period. The corpus of sealings found at Gilund is made up of 249 fragments of sealing clay, many of which had been impressed by stamp seals. The sealings were found primarily in contexts that can be dated to the Middle Ahar-Banas period. The majority (G.S. 4.001-4.214) of the 249 sealings from Gilund were unearthed during the fourth season (2002-2003). A second, smaller set of sealings (GS 1.001—1.008) was found in a large pit (lot 1014) during the first season of excavation (1999-2000). Other impressions were found singly throughout the excavated areas of GLD-2, but rarely in significant contexts. Most of the sealings found during season 5, for example, were found in contexts that can best be characterized as slope wash. The sealings were not given individual antiquity numbers when they were first excavated, but have since been given GS (Gilund Sealing) numbers. General Site Chronology and Highlights of the Excavations Beginning as a small village that was established ca. 3700 BC on an elevated river terrace between the Ravi and the old Beas Rivers, the ancient settlement we today designate as Harappa grew to become a small town with two major walled areas by ca. 2600 BC. Over the next 700 years during the Harappa Phase, ca. 2600-1900 BC, the city expanded with the construction of several walled suburbs and extra-mural occupation areas, covering an area of more than 100 and perhaps as much as 150 hectares (Meadow & Kenoyer 2005). The Early Harappan periods The Ravi Phase represents the initial occupation of the site (Period 1: ca. 3700 — ca. 2800 BC) and has cultural similarities with early settled communities in the Ghaggar-Hakra River valley to the east, as well as in many small regional cultures in the piedmont and highlands of Baluchistan to the west. Evidence from the analysis and sourcing of the raw materials used for chipped-stone and ground-stone manufacture, bead making, and shell bangle production indicate that the site was linked to distant resource areas throughout the Indus region (Kenoyer & Meadow 2000). Our excavations have recovered unfinished and finished seals from contexts some of which can be accurately dated and associated with specific activity areas at Harappa. Unfinished seals have been recovered from across the site, and through detailed comparisons, it may be possible to identify specific workshop styles and changes in carving techniques. Like the other Old World civilizations, the Indus Civilization seems to have grown from the skilful utilization of the fertile river valleys. Its distinctive characteristics - the gridiron layout of the cities, their elaborate drainage, and the puzzling pictographic script - are still best known from the excavations of Harappa and Mohenjodaro.! Three distinctive seals - representing the object type that has remained most characteristic of the Indus civilization - were found at Harappa in the Punjab and published in 1875, 1886 and 1912.2 But the full implication of these finds was not realized before excavations were started in 1920 at Harappa, and, by chance almost simultaneously, in 1922, at Mohenjo-daro in Sind, some 600 km south in the Indus valley. More seals of the same type were immediately found at both of these sites, and it became evident that an entirely unknown bronze-age civilization had come to light.3 This led to large-scale excavations at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa,* followed by much more limited digs at Chanhujo-daro further south in Sind.5 The bulk of the Indus (or Harappan) seals and inscriptions available to research comes from these excavations in the 1920's and 1930's. The enigma of the Indus script From the-very beginning, the enigmatic Indus script has been the most tantalizing one among the many problems presented by the Harappan culture. The short inscriptions hold an answer to the most debated question concerning this early urban culture, that concerning its language. Many attempts at deciphering this unknown writing system have been made ever since the first specimen was published in 1875, and all sorts of 'solutions' have been proposed. But no unanimity has been reached even on the basic issues. The label "Early Harappan” is used in this volume in its now widely current conventional sense first suggested in 1970 by Dr M. Rafique Mughal, i.e. as corresponding to "Kot Dijian" and dated to c. 3000-2500 B.C. The term implies that there is an unbroken cultural continuity between this "Early Harappan" phase and the following "Mature Harappan" phase dated to c. 2500-2000 B.C.3 While "Mature Harappan" is usually understood to be a synonym for the fully urbanized Indus Civilization possessed of the Indus script, in the sites of the Northwestern Frontier Province like Hissam-dheri or Gumla it is rather a temporal designation of the cultural phase, which in many respects remains similar to the "Early Harappan" phase. Thus most of the graffiti coming from Hissam-dheri and Gumla seem to represent "potter's marks” rather than the Indus script. We take the opportunity of summarizing in this short note some of the main topics and reasons of interest of this important class of finds. General Issues The large early urban site of Shahr-i Sokhta, in the first half of the 3rd millennium BC, appeared as a dense cluster of private dwellings looking out into a haphazard network of dusty alleys. As life thrived and the city grew, large dumps were piled up in vacant lots, while sediments spilled over floors and living surfaces. This required a constant process of rebuilding, in which pavements were raised with fills largely made of ceramics, while roofs were rebuilt at a higher level on top of each room. For these reasons, although some erections (particularly those destroyed by a wide-scale destructive event at the end of Period I) were sealed in contexts of primary firing and collapse, Period II buildings are entirely filled with secondary layers and fillings, and it is quite problematic to refer artifacts, among them seals and sealings, to their primary architectural and functional associations (unbaked clay sealings in this regard are better evidence, because of their ephemeral and fragile materiality). The wide corpus of complete vessels belonging to these periods indicates clearly that there is no link between the marks and the quality or function of the pots. Neither are they indicators of capacity. The large proportion of pots not incised with marks and the study of the ceramic material found in situ in several storage rooms does not suggest concepts such as means of facilitating some kind of registration after firing, or of trademarks, and it does not argue for the possibility that the marks served to identify the individual who owned the pots. The true nature of the marking system was perhaps required not when the pots were in use, but before, during the manufacturing cycle, between the final stage of forming and the moment the vessels stacked in the kiln were removed from it after firing.’ As regards manufacturing, it is interesting to note that the finest examples of the potter’s craft come from those periods whose craftsmen had perfected firing techniques (e.g., the coated jars used as saggars) and decorating techniques (e.g., splendidly decorated Grey Ware). There is a range of remarkable pots beautifully decorated with a vast repertoire of complex painted designs showing the skill of the potters and the particular care involved in their production. During the subsequent Period I C (2700 BC) at Nausharo at the time when the use of incised marks decrease considerably important changes in pottery manufacture are noticed. A new kiln type appears during that period. Many examples were excavated at Lal Shah, a site located near Mehrgarh, where the pottery was similar in all respects to that of Nausharo Period I C (Pracchia 1985). The kilns are double chambered, and in the middle of the combustion chamber stood a column which supported the perforated floor of a firing chamber holding the pots to be fired. The kilns were grouped in rows on two levels. They resemble more recent firing structures of Mohenjo-daro or Harappa as well as kilns uncovered at Nausharo in the mature Indus levels of Period HI. While the Archaeological Survey continued to operate in India, in Pakistan the Department of Archaeology and Museums had to be created from scratch. chunk_text: Inscribed Objects from Harappa Excavations 1986-2007 J. MARK KENOYER RICHARD H. MEADOW Introduction Ever since the discovery of the first engraved seals of the Indus Civilization at the site of Harappa, scholars have been trying to unlock the secrets of the Indus script’ and to understand the social, economic, and political importance of these and other inscribed objects. Although the inscriptions have remained undeciphered, it has been possible to gain some insight into the context for the use of the script based on carefully documented recovery of inscribed objects from recent excavations throughout the greater Indus region. In this volume, we present for the first time in one place the assemblage of inscribed and incised objects discovered at the site of Harappa during excavations conducted between 1986-2007 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP)’. ' That “writing” and “script” are appropriate terms to employ in reference to what has commonly been called the “Indus script” has been contested by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004). They argue that the Indus script is not likely to have been linked directly to a spoken language and was probably a system of non-linguistic symbols. We, however, contend that given the development in the system of inscriptions over time as seen at Harappa and given the extensive use of the “signs” or “symbols” both formally and informally and on many media (see text discussion), making the distinction between a language-based script and a not-so-tied-to-language symboling system is not a particularly interesting distinction. In any event, in the absence of multi-lingual texts, long texts, and/or a successor symboling system or script, there can be no widely accepted understanding of what the symbols or signs of the “Indus script” actually meant to those who employed them, and thus there can be no true resolution of this issue. As a result, we continue to employ terms like “script” and even “writing” in their broadest senses and are well aware that not everyone may agree with such usage. We are also rather imprecise in our use of the terms “inscribed” and “inscription”, which we employ broadly in relation to the Indus script and not in the restricted sense of something engraved, incised, or written. Thus pieces with script in relief are also referred to as inscribed (although not “incised”).

A note on the material and production of the objects and on the colour photographs Space forbids discussing the material and production of the Indus seals and inscriptions in any detail here; for this the reader is once again referred to the excavation reports. It can only be noted that the great majority of the Indus seals are made of steatite, generally whitish in colour. The seals were first sawed and cut into their forms and then polished; the subject was outlined with a sharp point and then engraved with a drill. Finally the seal was coated with an alkali and heated. It seems that the alkali coating was applied mainly to dark steatite in order to make it white. Heating hardens the steatite, which is a very soft stone, and thus protects it against wear. The various stages of this process can been seen from different examples, the unfinished ones being particularly instructive. 109 The moulded tablets are normally made of terracotta or faience, while the incised tablets usually are of steatite or copper. Indus seals and the external contacts of the Indus Civilization Immediately after the first news about the discovery of the Indus Civilization was published in 1924, it became apparent that the Harappans had been in contact with the ancient Western Asiatic cultures. Evidence for this was Indus seals coming from Susa, Ur, and other Mesopotamian sites; among these were both square stamp seals of a purely native Harappan type and seals combining Harappan and local elements such as the cylinder form. Later, a few round Indus seals (a type rarely found in the Indus Valley) were discovered along with a large number of local round stamp seals on the islands of Failaka and Bahrain in the Gulf, where excavations since the 1950's have revealed a flourishing "Dilmun Civilization". Three foreign countries are referred to as participants of the sea trade: Dilmun (closest to Mesopotamia), Magan and (farthest away) Meluhha. Magan is now widely identified with Oman and the opposite coast of Makran, and Meluhha with the Harappan realm.®! The excavations of Mehrgarh, Nausharo and Sibri along with their analytical interpretation by J.-F. Jarrige and his team have created a firm basis for understanding cultural evolution in the Indo-Iranian borderlands, and provided a continuous archaeological sequence from the Neolithic to the Iron Age. With regard to the origins of the Indus Civilization, one must also mention the publication of J.-M. Casal’s excavations (1962-65) at Nindowari along with a documentation of the Kulli culture ceramics coming from recently looted graveyards (J.-F. Jarrige et al. 2011). In their conclusion, J.-F. Jarrige and his colleagues emphasize that the Kulli culture had already fully developed by 2600 BCE, before the formation of the Indus Civilization between 2600 and 2500 BCE. The Kulli culture also retained its separate identity in southern Baluchistan until 1900 BCE. The animal iconography of the Kulli pots goes back to earlier local traditions and includes as one of its important motifs “bull tied to a kind of post or tree”. The scene greatly resembles the most important iconographic motif of the Indus seals, the “unicorn” bull standing in front of a peculiar stand. Bulls tethered to fig trees are a prominent motif also at Nausharo I D, immediately preceding the Harappan Period Nausharo II. Evidently the roots of the Indus Civilization are in the earlier cultures of the Indo-Iranian borderlands, which in turn are connected with the cultures of the eastern half of the Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia. This wide area remained an interaction sphere even in Harappan times (Lamberg-Karlovsky & Tosi 1973; Cortesi et al. 2008; J.-F. A computer-drawn concordance to the Indus inscriptions was published in 1973 by a group of Finnish scholars.4> In the preparation of this work, Dr Asko Parpola visited the principal museums in Pakistan and India in 1971 in order to compare the readings based on the published photographs with the original objects. To his surprise he found more than 400 seals and inscriptions from Mohenjo-daro and Harappa that had never been published.46 Most of them came from the digs carried out by the custodians of the site museums after the official excavations and reported only very briefly in the Annual Reports of the ASI.47 (Fortunately, the unpublished fieldbooks of these as well as of the official excavations have since been discovered in Pakistan, and are in the process of being published.48) Mr Mahadevan brought out his edition and concordance of the texts in the Indus script in 1977, improving upon the Finnish concordance in several respects.4? Besides, Mahadevan could include more text material on the basis of the Photo Archive of the ASI, which preserves old unpublished photographs of objects since lost. On the other hand, however, Mahadevan excluded all material that Asko Parpola had discovered in the museums of Pakistan and that had been included in the Finnish concordance. Mahadevan's book further included a listing of the texts on which the concordance is based, good documentation, and several cross charts with interesting statistics of different kinds. Dr Parpola had gone through the Photo Archive of the ASI in 1975 and identified most of its material. In collaboration with Dr Kimmo Koskenniemi, he brought out a revised edition of the Finnish concordance in three volumes in 1979-1982, since there was still scope for improving upon the reading of the inscriptions and upon Mahadevan's work. The main reason for this unfortunate state of affairs is the fact that all keys that opened other unknown scripts are unavailable here. There are no bi- or multilingual inscriptions giving the same text in both Indus script and some readable characters. There are no understood historical texts which could tell the names of the Harappan gods, kings or cities, or which would quote samples of the language spoken by the Indus people. It can only be noted that the great majority of the Indus seals are made of steatite, generally whitish in colour. The seals were first sawed and cut into their forms and then polished; the subject was outlined with a sharp point and then engraved with a drill. chunk_text: XXVI INTRODUCTION Ernest Mackay, in Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro, arranged the objects coming from Mohenjo-daro according to the different areas of the site and the absolute depth of the finding place from the surface.68 He wished to control the data from the point of view of archaeological distribution, looking for evolutionary and other trends. The result was chaotic: objects of different types and sizes were mixed with each other. Unless one knows the number of the object, it is impossible to locate it without scanning through the entire material. In the present Corpus, the archaeological context is taken into account in the arrangement of the objects when it is feasible and useful: thus the objects from the Late Harappan period from Lothal (graffiti only) and Chanhujo-daro (seals) are presented as a separate section at the end. The aim of the classification must be efficiency in placing and locating any given object within the whole. The type of the object, form, material, iconographic motif, size, style and state of preservation have been chosen as parameters in the Corpus, in this order. A solution of this kind, which makes a neat layout possible, was followed by Sir John Marshall in Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization and, less successfully, by M.S.Vats in Excavations at Harappa. The lst criterion: the owners of the objects; and the overall publication plan Ideally, of course, one would like to see all the objects coming from a single site, for example Mohenjo-daro, neatly arranged into one single sequence. There are, however, other considerations and realities, which have made it impracticable to realize this ideal. Instead, the Corpus is divided into three volumes according to. the first criterion of physical location and ownership of the original objects. In this the Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions follows the example of the Corpus of Minoan and Mycenean Seals, for instance, which is divided into different volumes according to the museums in which seals are preserved. chunk_text: order to understand better the formation process of the Indus Civilization and the background of its seals, including foreign seals found in Harappan contexts, it seems necessary to widen the scope of CISI to include also seals discovered in archaeological excavations of prehistoric eastern Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia (excluding the great multitude of seals that come from looted graves of these regions). An important site, with seals closely related to those of Mundigak and Mehrgarh, is Shahr-i Sokhta, the capital of the “Helmand Civilization” of ancient Seistan. Massimo Vidale and Alessandra Lazzari, who participated in the excavations of Shahr-i Sokhta and are in charge of the excavation archives, immediately agreed to my proposal to collect the published glyptic material from Shahr-i Sokhta and include it in this volume. They also wrote an introductory essay and sent me relevant publications not accessible in Helsinki. Period I at Shahr-i Sokhta, dated to the early third millennium BCE, witnesses the presence of Proto-Elamites at the site, using Mesopotamian-type cylinder seals, while the local ceramics are related to the Damb-Sadaat/Quetta Ware distributed right to the borders of the Indus Valley. Shahr-i Sokhta was the easternmost point of the Uruk Expansion until Roland Besenval (2011: 49-51 & 133, figs. 121-122) brought to light typically Proto-Elamite bevel-rimmed vessels at Mir-i Qalat in Pakistani Baluchistan. The cylinder seals disappear after Period I, and Period II at Shahr-i Sokhta starts with the introduction of stone and metal seals and related ceramics, apparently coming from southern Turkmenistan (Geoksyur I / Namazga III). As many seals and sealings from Shahr-i Sokhta have not been assigned to definite periods, the material has been arranged typologically. The site of Chanhu-daro, in lower Sindh, was excavated by Ernest Mackay in 1935-36 (CE, 1943). Most of the finds remained in India, and the seals from Chanhu-daro in the care of the ASI were published in CISI 1. Many seals and other objects, however, could be taken to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (BMFA), which had been financing the excavation. These seals from Chanhu-daro are published in this volume with the excellent photographs provided by the BMFA. chunk_text: Authority Structure and the Evolution of Early Writing Systems Reclassifying the Indus Script Through Comparative Administrative Typology Abstract The Indus script has long been treated as an anomalous or incomplete writing system due to its short inscriptions, lack of phonetic decipherment, and apparent disappearance without textual descendants. This paper proposes a reclassification of the Indus script as a fully realized nonphonetic administrative operator system, optimized for governance within a distributed trade network rather than a centralized state. By identifying a shared semantic operator grammar across the Indus script, early Mesopotamian cuneiform, and early Chinese writing, and by testing this grammar against control cases from Shang oracle bone inscriptions and early Mesopotamian administrative tablets, this study demonstrates that divergence in script evolution correlates with authority topology, not cognitive or cultural capacity. The Indus script is shown to terminate at a point of functional sufficiency aligned with network authority, rather than failing to evolve toward language. 1. The Problem of the Indus Script Despite more than a century of study, the Indus script remains undeciphered in phonetic terms. Its inscriptions are short, highly repetitive, and largely confined to seals and a small number of public signboards. Traditional expectations that writing systems evolve toward phonetic representation, narrative expression, and historical memory have led to the Indus script being framed as primitive, incomplete, or interrupted by civilizational collapse. This framing assumes that linguistic encoding is the natural endpoint of writing. However, comparative evidence from other early writing systems suggests that writing initially emerges not as language, but as administrative technology. This paper argues that the Indus script should be evaluated according to the functional demands of its authority structure rather than by comparison to later literary traditions. 2. MEADOW Introduction Ever since the discovery of the first engraved seals of the Indus Civilization at the site of Harappa, scholars have been trying to unlock the secrets of the Indus script’ and to understand the social, economic, and political importance of these and other inscribed objects. Although the inscriptions have remained undeciphered, it has been possible to gain some insight into the context for the use of the script based on carefully documented recovery of inscribed objects from recent excavations throughout the greater Indus region. In this volume, we present for the first time in one place the assemblage of inscribed and incised objects discovered at the site of Harappa during excavations conducted between 1986-2007 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP)’. ' That “writing” and “script” are appropriate terms to employ in reference to what has commonly been called the “Indus script” has been contested by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004). They argue that the Indus script is not likely to have been linked directly to a spoken language and was probably a system of non-linguistic symbols. We, however, contend that given the development in the system of inscriptions over time as seen at Harappa and given the extensive use of the “signs” or “symbols” both formally and informally and on many media (see text discussion), making the distinction between a language-based script and a not-so-tied-to-language symboling system is not a particularly interesting distinction. In any event, in the absence of multi-lingual texts, long texts, and/or a successor symboling system or script, there can be no widely accepted understanding of what the symbols or signs of the “Indus script” actually meant to those who employed them, and thus there can be no true resolution of this issue. As a result, we continue to employ terms like “script” and even “writing” in their broadest senses and are well aware that not everyone may agree with such usage. We are also rather imprecise in our use of the terms “inscribed” and “inscription”, which we employ broadly in relation to the Indus script and not in the restricted sense of something engraved, incised, or written. Thus pieces with script in relief are also referred to as inscribed (although not “incised”).

chunk_text: 6. Why the Indus Script Terminates Under this framework, the Indus script does not fail to evolve. It terminates correctly. • No centralized courts require narrative law • No empire requires phonetic standardization • No archival bureaucracy requires long-term memory • High population heterogeneity favors signage over speech Writing systems evolve toward the minimum structure required by authority. The Indus script reached that minimum and stopped. 7. Scope and Non-Claims This paper does not propose: • a phonetic decipherment of the Indus script • linguistic ancestry or diffusion between writing systems • cultural borrowing or influence • translation of individual glyphs The contribution is classificatory, not lexical. 8. Conclusion The Indus script represents a coherent and fully functional non-phonetic administrative writing system optimized for governance within a distributed trade network. Comparative testing against early Chinese and Mesopotamian writing demonstrates that early scripts share a semantic operator grammar and diverge predictably according to authority topology. This reframing resolves longstanding misconceptions about the Indus script and situates it within a broader, testable typology of early writing systems.

The main reason for this unfortunate state of affairs is the fact that all keys that opened other unknown scripts are unavailable here. There are no bi- or multilingual inscriptions giving the same text in both Indus script and some readable characters. MEADOW Introduction Ever since the discovery of the first engraved seals of the Indus Civilization at the site of Harappa, scholars have been trying to unlock the secrets of the Indus script’ and to understand the social, economic, and political importance of these and other inscribed objects. Although the inscriptions have remained undeciphered, it has been possible to gain some insight into the context for the use of the script based on carefully documented recovery of inscribed objects from recent excavations throughout the greater Indus region. In this volume, we present for the first time in one place the assemblage of inscribed and incised objects discovered at the site of Harappa during excavations conducted between 1986-2007 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP)’. ' That “writing” and “script” are appropriate terms to employ in reference to what has commonly been called the “Indus script” has been contested by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004). They argue that the Indus script is not likely to have been linked directly to a spoken language and was probably a system of non-linguistic symbols. We, however, contend that given the development in the system of inscriptions over time as seen at Harappa and given the extensive use of the “signs” or “symbols” both formally and informally and on many media (see text discussion), making the distinction between a language-based script and a not-so-tied-to-language symboling system is not a particularly interesting distinction. In any event, in the absence of multi-lingual texts, long texts, and/or a successor symboling system or script, there can be no widely accepted understanding of what the symbols or signs of the “Indus script” actually meant to those who employed them, and thus there can be no true resolution of this issue. As a result, we continue to employ terms like “script” and even “writing” in their broadest senses and are well aware that not everyone may agree with such usage. We are also rather imprecise in our use of the terms “inscribed” and “inscription”, which we employ broadly in relation to the Indus script and not in the restricted sense of something engraved, incised, or written. Thus pieces with script in relief are also referred to as inscribed (although not “incised”).

There is an apparent increase in the number of sign types from Period IV to Period VII B of Mehrgarh and the contemporary Period I B of Nausharo. These periods witness the greatest use of incised signs: one pot out of four was then marked. The signs are much less frequent in the subsequent pre-Indus Periods I C and I D (2700-2500 BCE). While the use of signs on Indus seals is fairly well studied, until recently there have been no systematic studies of their use on other kinds of objects due to the small numbers of such objects or their fragmentary nature. These different kinds of inscribed artifacts are now being studied spatially and chronologically and compared with seals from similar contexts and periods. Although we are still only at the beginning of this study, it seems that signs on seals and tablets usually reflect a more formal use of the script while those on other artifacts may be more informal and even, in some cases, represent the more spontaneous use of various signs. Spontaneity is particularly likely for graffiti on ceramic vessels, which were incised with script after manufacturing and firing. This use of signs clearly demonstrates that it was not only craftsmen commissioned to prepare formal devices who incised the script, but also others who employed it directly to label a container with perhaps one or more of the following: the name of its owner, the nature of its contents, its origin, its destination, or an incantation — to name some of the more obvious possibilities. Rarely this type of boss has a double groove, as at the site of Gola Dhoro (Bagasara), Gujarat (Bhan et al. 2005). The perforation is generally oriented horizontally in the same direction as the script and animal motif. The drilling for the perforation is done from both sides and angled down so that the hole meets deep inside the seal body rather than at the level of the boss itself. This drilling tech- _ nique was necessary to avoid weakening the small area where the boss joins the seal body. Nevertheless, a common form of seal breakage is detachment of the boss because of the weak structure of steatite itself.'* Another form of boss found during Harappa Phase Periods 3B and 3C is usually on steatite seals with geometric designs such as circle and dot motifs (H-1700, H-1702). The boss is a simple raised square with a flat or convex surface and a transverse perforation. Similar types of bosses are found on a variety of faience button seals also dated to Periods 3B/C and 3C. During the final phase of the Harappan occupation (Period 3C) the single grooved boss continues to be used on square seals. On the long rectangular seals, however, there is no separate knob, with the perforation being drilled transversely through the sides of the central and thickest part of the seal.'? There are a few exceptions to this pattern and two of the long rectangular seals recovered in earlier excavations from Harappa have a grooved knob or boss on the back (CISI 1, p. 203: H-161, H-162). Another form of boss that appears in period 3C is a domed or convex form found on square geometric seals. The domed back is usually decorated with concentric circles or floral motifs. MEADOW Introduction Ever since the discovery of the first engraved seals of the Indus Civilization at the site of Harappa, scholars have been trying to unlock the secrets of the Indus script’ and to understand the social, economic, and political importance of these and other inscribed objects. Although the inscriptions have remained undeciphered, it has been possible to gain some insight into the context for the use of the script based on carefully documented recovery of inscribed objects from recent excavations throughout the greater Indus region. In this volume, we present for the first time in one place the assemblage of inscribed and incised objects discovered at the site of Harappa during excavations conducted between 1986-2007 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP)’. ' That “writing” and “script” are appropriate terms to employ in reference to what has commonly been called the “Indus script” has been contested by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004). They argue that the Indus script is not likely to have been linked directly to a spoken language and was probably a system of non-linguistic symbols. We, however, contend that given the development in the system of inscriptions over time as seen at Harappa and given the extensive use of the “signs” or “symbols” both formally and informally and on many media (see text discussion), making the distinction between a language-based script and a not-so-tied-to-language symboling system is not a particularly interesting distinction. In any event, in the absence of multi-lingual texts, long texts, and/or a successor symboling system or script, there can be no widely accepted understanding of what the symbols or signs of the “Indus script” actually meant to those who employed them, and thus there can be no true resolution of this issue. As a result, we continue to employ terms like “script” and even “writing” in their broadest senses and are well aware that not everyone may agree with such usage. We are also rather imprecise in our use of the terms “inscribed” and “inscription”, which we employ broadly in relation to the Indus script and not in the restricted sense of something engraved, incised, or written. Thus pieces with script in relief are also referred to as inscribed (although not “incised”).

chunk_text: our recent work at Harappa has focused on understanding the details of cultural developments during Periods 3B and 3C. Results reveal these to have been dynamic periods of urban expansion together with recurrent decay, rebuilding, and reorganization in different parts of the city. In 2000 and 2001, excavations turned to recovering more information on Period 3A in order to reveal initial Harappa Phase developments, particularly relating to the use of inscribed pieces. This period is poorly represented in excavations at most Indus sites, because the remains are buried under later occupation levels. At Harappa, it has been possible to recover two seal fragments from Period 3A, providing an important baseline against which to evaluate stylistic and technological change in the use of seals (see below for more discussion). Based on evidence at hand to date, square seals with script together with the unicorn or other animal motifs are associated primarily with the Tater part of Period 3A and are relatively common throughout Period 3B and on into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997). Square seals with script alone are found first in Period 3B, but long rectangular seals with script alone are confined to Period 3C. We are also obtaining important chronological information with respect to inscribed tablets, which are particularly common at Harappa, more so than the seals. Through careful stratigraphic cutting-back of Vats’ section in Trench I of Mound F and comparison with his report of that trench (Vats 1940), we have determined that he was not correct in reporting that small steatite tablets with incised script are from the earliest levels of the site. Instead it is evident that such tablets appeared toward the middle of Period 3B and continued to be used well into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). Furthermore, these inscribed steatite tablets, which Vats (1940) called “tiny steatite seals”, are not seals at all but are incised with script that was to be read directly from the tablet. Whether there were parallel changes in the script needs to be investigated in detail. In the past, studies of the Indus script have lumped all of the best-preserved seal inscriptions together and used this combined assemblage as the basis for a study of the script. Based on the discoveries at Harappa, it is now possible for that site at least to separate out different chronological periods of seal production and to compare seal inscriptions with those found on other types of objects such as incised and molded tablets and pottery, which together greatly outnumber the seals and seal impressions recovered from the site. The use of Indus signs on distinctive types of objects as well as upon ornaments and pottery indicates common cultural practice at sites of the Indus Civilization. This shared practice may be a reflection of or have played a role in the integration of populations within and between urban centers as well as with communities spread out across rural areas, along trade routes, and in resource areas. Especially as new excavations produce stratigraphically controlled and well-dated inscribed pieces, it becomes both possible and increasingly important that the script and accompanying iconography be subjected to rigorous analysis at the site, regional, and cross-regional levels to investigate trends of change through time and variability across space. When such studies have been carried out, assumptions about the uniformity of the signing system (Parpola 1994) probably will need to be revised. Even though these new discoveries will not lead to a decipherment of the Indus script, any new patterns that can be discerned at Harappa and at other sites where close stratigraphic and spatial documentation has been possible, will help us to better interpret the role of the script in the Indus world. In our opinion, too much scholarly (and lay) emphasis has been placed on the unattainable goal of decipherment of the Indus script and not enough on treating seals, tablets, and other inscribed materials as archaeological finds that went through processes of materials selection, production, use, and discard. It can only be noted that the great majority of the Indus seals are made of steatite, generally whitish in colour. The seals were first sawed and cut into their forms and then polished; the subject was outlined with a sharp point and then engraved with a drill. Finally the seal was coated with an alkali and heated. It seems that the alkali coating was applied mainly to dark steatite in order to make it white. Heating hardens the steatite, which is a very soft stone, and thus protects it against wear. chunk_text: 6. Why the Indus Script Terminates Under this framework, the Indus script does not fail to evolve. It terminates correctly. • No centralized courts require narrative law • No empire requires phonetic standardization • No archival bureaucracy requires long-term memory • High population heterogeneity favors signage over speech Writing systems evolve toward the minimum structure required by authority. The Indus script reached that minimum and stopped. 7. Scope and Non-Claims This paper does not propose: • a phonetic decipherment of the Indus script • linguistic ancestry or diffusion between writing systems • cultural borrowing or influence • translation of individual glyphs The contribution is classificatory, not lexical. 8. Conclusion The Indus script represents a coherent and fully functional non-phonetic administrative writing system optimized for governance within a distributed trade network. Comparative testing against early Chinese and Mesopotamian writing demonstrates that early scripts share a semantic operator grammar and diverge predictably according to authority topology. This reframing resolves longstanding misconceptions about the Indus script and situates it within a broader, testable typology of early writing systems.

chunk_text: Authority Structure and the Evolution of Early Writing Systems Reclassifying the Indus Script Through Comparative Administrative Typology Abstract The Indus script has long been treated as an anomalous or incomplete writing system due to its short inscriptions, lack of phonetic decipherment, and apparent disappearance without textual descendants. This paper proposes a reclassification of the Indus script as a fully realized nonphonetic administrative operator system, optimized for governance within a distributed trade network rather than a centralized state. By identifying a shared semantic operator grammar across the Indus script, early Mesopotamian cuneiform, and early Chinese writing, and by testing this grammar against control cases from Shang oracle bone inscriptions and early Mesopotamian administrative tablets, this study demonstrates that divergence in script evolution correlates with authority topology, not cognitive or cultural capacity. The Indus script is shown to terminate at a point of functional sufficiency aligned with network authority, rather than failing to evolve toward language. 1. The Problem of the Indus Script Despite more than a century of study, the Indus script remains undeciphered in phonetic terms. Its inscriptions are short, highly repetitive, and largely confined to seals and a small number of public signboards. Traditional expectations that writing systems evolve toward phonetic representation, narrative expression, and historical memory have led to the Indus script being framed as primitive, incomplete, or interrupted by civilizational collapse. This framing assumes that linguistic encoding is the natural endpoint of writing. However, comparative evidence from other early writing systems suggests that writing initially emerges not as language, but as administrative technology. This paper argues that the Indus script should be evaluated according to the functional demands of its authority structure rather than by comparison to later literary traditions. 2. Incised and Painted Marks on the Pottery of Mehrgarh and Nausharo-Baluchistan XXV Many symbols are common to the various sites.2 But this visible similarity of signs is most probably due to the use, in each corpus, of a range of simple geometric designs which are also comparable with many symbols occurring in elaborate writing systems. Many signs have parallels in the proto-Elamite script ( fig. 1, sign no. 82 and fig. 2, signs no. 20, 21, 22, 28, 34, A1, 43 and 45) as well as with many basic signs of the Indus script (Parpola 1994). The relationship between the two writing systems has often been suggested by the possibility of a link through the pre-Indus incised marks on pottery (Potts 1981).2 But many comparable marks from Susiana or Mehrgarh IV are dated earlier than the creation of the proto-Elamite system and similar pre-firing marks were still incised on vessels at a time when the Indus script was already known. This continuity of use of pre-firing marks, although much less frequently, seems to argue against the hypothesis that the roots of the Indus script are in the incised marks tradition of some predecessors. The simple designs of the comparable pre-existing signs, easily produced by a tool or a stylus, may be the reason why they were adopted, intentionally or not, in the Indus script. The pre-firing marks are always single signs and the assumption that they may have been part or variants of even a crude form of writing cannot be proved, but they probably represent a system of mutually intelligible symbols commonly accepted through time and space, and it seems likely that these incised marks were merely utilitarian. A computer-drawn concordance to the Indus inscriptions was published in 1973 by a group of Finnish scholars.4> In the preparation of this work, Dr Asko Parpola visited the principal museums in Pakistan and India in 1971 in order to compare the readings based on the published photographs with the original objects. To his surprise he found more than 400 seals and inscriptions from Mohenjo-daro and Harappa that had never been published.46 Most of them came from the digs carried out by the custodians of the site museums after the official excavations and reported only very briefly in the Annual Reports of the ASI.47 (Fortunately, the unpublished fieldbooks of these as well as of the official excavations have since been discovered in Pakistan, and are in the process of being published.48) Mr Mahadevan brought out his edition and concordance of the texts in the Indus script in 1977, improving upon the Finnish concordance in several respects.4? Besides, Mahadevan could include more text material on the basis of the Photo Archive of the ASI, which preserves old unpublished photographs of objects since lost. On the other hand, however, Mahadevan excluded all material that Asko Parpola had discovered in the museums of Pakistan and that had been included in the Finnish concordance. Mahadevan's book further included a listing of the texts on which the concordance is based, good documentation, and several cross charts with interesting statistics of different kinds. Dr Parpola had gone through the Photo Archive of the ASI in 1975 and identified most of its material. In collaboration with Dr Kimmo Koskenniemi, he brought out a revised edition of the Finnish concordance in three volumes in 1979-1982, since there was still scope for improving upon the reading of the inscriptions and upon Mahadevan's work. chunk_text: Authority Structure and the Evolution of Early Writing Systems Reclassifying the Indus Script Through Comparative Administrative Typology Abstract The Indus script has long been treated as an anomalous or incomplete writing system due to its short inscriptions, lack of phonetic decipherment, and apparent disappearance without textual descendants. This paper proposes a reclassification of the Indus script as a fully realized nonphonetic administrative operator system, optimized for governance within a distributed trade network rather than a centralized state. By identifying a shared semantic operator grammar across the Indus script, early Mesopotamian cuneiform, and early Chinese writing, and by testing this grammar against control cases from Shang oracle bone inscriptions and early Mesopotamian administrative tablets, this study demonstrates that divergence in script evolution correlates with authority topology, not cognitive or cultural capacity. The Indus script is shown to terminate at a point of functional sufficiency aligned with network authority, rather than failing to evolve toward language. 1. The Problem of the Indus Script Despite more than a century of study, the Indus script remains undeciphered in phonetic terms. Its inscriptions are short, highly repetitive, and largely confined to seals and a small number of public signboards. Traditional expectations that writing systems evolve toward phonetic representation, narrative expression, and historical memory have led to the Indus script being framed as primitive, incomplete, or interrupted by civilizational collapse. This framing assumes that linguistic encoding is the natural endpoint of writing. However, comparative evidence from other early writing systems suggests that writing initially emerges not as language, but as administrative technology. This paper argues that the Indus script should be evaluated according to the functional demands of its authority structure rather than by comparison to later literary traditions. 2. chunk_text: 6. Why the Indus Script Terminates Under this framework, the Indus script does not fail to evolve. It terminates correctly. • No centralized courts require narrative law • No empire requires phonetic standardization • No archival bureaucracy requires long-term memory • High population heterogeneity favors signage over speech Writing systems evolve toward the minimum structure required by authority. The Indus script reached that minimum and stopped. 7. Scope and Non-Claims This paper does not propose: • a phonetic decipherment of the Indus script • linguistic ancestry or diffusion between writing systems • cultural borrowing or influence • translation of individual glyphs The contribution is classificatory, not lexical. 8. Conclusion The Indus script represents a coherent and fully functional non-phonetic administrative writing system optimized for governance within a distributed trade network. Comparative testing against early Chinese and Mesopotamian writing demonstrates that early scripts share a semantic operator grammar and diverge predictably according to authority topology. This reframing resolves longstanding misconceptions about the Indus script and situates it within a broader, testable typology of early writing systems.

Whether there were parallel changes in the script needs to be investigated in detail. In the past, studies of the Indus script have lumped all of the best-preserved seal inscriptions together and used this combined assemblage as the basis for a study of the script. Based on the discoveries at Harappa, it is now possible for that site at least to separate out different chronological periods of seal production and to compare seal inscriptions with those found on other types of objects such as incised and molded tablets and pottery, which together greatly outnumber the seals and seal impressions recovered from the site. The use of Indus signs on distinctive types of objects as well as upon ornaments and pottery indicates common cultural practice at sites of the Indus Civilization. This shared practice may be a reflection of or have played a role in the integration of populations within and between urban centers as well as with communities spread out across rural areas, along trade routes, and in resource areas. Especially as new excavations produce stratigraphically controlled and well-dated inscribed pieces, it becomes both possible and increasingly important that the script and accompanying iconography be subjected to rigorous analysis at the site, regional, and cross-regional levels to investigate trends of change through time and variability across space. When such studies have been carried out, assumptions about the uniformity of the signing system (Parpola 1994) probably will need to be revised. Even though these new discoveries will not lead to a decipherment of the Indus script, any new patterns that can be discerned at Harappa and at other sites where close stratigraphic and spatial documentation has been possible, will help us to better interpret the role of the script in the Indus world. The purpose and scope of the Corpus The texts in standardized editions and corcordances are based upon the subjective judgements of individual scholars, and they do not display all the intricacies of the originals. Moreover, they contain numerous admittedly doubtful readings. Objective photographic documentation of the original inscriptions thus is a necessary complement to such textual studies. Photographs of the original objects are equally indispensable tools for the historians of art and religion studying the iconographic motifs and for archaeologists engaged in a comparative study of the objects. In short, there is no replacement for good photographs of all the Indus seals and inscriptions. A major part of the material has been published in photographs in the excavation reports of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa: they illustrate altogether roughly 2500 objects. These publications have long been out of print and difficult to procure. There are no bi- or multilingual inscriptions giving the same text in both Indus script and some readable characters. chunk_text: Analysis of early writing systems reveals a common semantic structure preceding phoneticization. Across the Indus script, early Mesopotamian cuneiform, and early Chinese inscriptions, inscriptions can be decomposed into a recurring sequence of functional operators: 1. ENTITY – the object, asset, or subject being governed 2. DOMAIN / JURISDICTION – the spatial, institutional, or ritual scope of authority 3. PROCESS – the action performed on or involving the entity 4. STATE / QUALIFIER – conditional or status information 5. TERMINATION / AUTHORIZATION – closure, validation, or binding force This operator grammar appears consistently in the earliest administrative contexts and does not depend on phonetic representation. Meaning emerges from position, combination, and repetition rather than from encoded speech. 3. Authority Topology as the Divergence Variable While the administrative core is shared, writing systems diverge predictably based on authority topology. 3.1 Network Authority: The Indus Case The Indus Valley Civilization exhibits a highly distributed structure characterized by multiple trade hubs, standardized material culture, and the absence of clear evidence for centralized rulership. In this context, writing functions to stabilize processes rather than preserve speech or memory. Key features of the Indus script follow directly: • non-phonetic, operator-based signs • minimal numeracy • short, modular inscriptions • compatibility with seals and public signage • no narrative or historical record Once administrative sufficiency is reached, further elaboration provides no functional advantage. 3.2 Institutional Authority: Mesopotamia Early Mesopotamian writing emerges in temple and palace contexts where surplus management, auditability, and accountability are critical. While early cuneiform shares the same operator grammar, it rapidly expands numerically and develops phonetic supplements to resolve disputes, track individuals, and preserve records over time.

Indus seals and the external contacts of the Indus Civilization Immediately after the first news about the discovery of the Indus Civilization was published in 1924, it became apparent that the Harappans had been in contact with the ancient Western Asiatic cultures. Evidence for this was Indus seals coming from Susa, Ur, and other Mesopotamian sites; among these were both square stamp seals of a purely native Harappan type and seals combining Harappan and local elements such as the cylinder form. Later, a few round Indus seals (a type rarely found in the Indus Valley) were discovered along with a large number of local round stamp seals on the islands of Failaka and Bahrain in the Gulf, where excavations since the 1950's have revealed a flourishing "Dilmun Civilization". The excavations of Mehrgarh, Nausharo and Sibri along with their analytical interpretation by J.-F. Jarrige and his team have created a firm basis for understanding cultural evolution in the Indo-Iranian borderlands, and provided a continuous archaeological sequence from the Neolithic to the Iron Age. With regard to the origins of the Indus Civilization, one must also mention the publication of J.-M. Casal’s excavations (1962-65) at Nindowari along with a documentation of the Kulli culture ceramics coming from recently looted graveyards (J.-F. Jarrige et al. 2011). In their conclusion, J.-F. Jarrige and his colleagues emphasize that the Kulli culture had already fully developed by 2600 BCE, before the formation of the Indus Civilization between 2600 and 2500 BCE. The Kulli culture also retained its separate identity in southern Baluchistan until 1900 BCE. The animal iconography of the Kulli pots goes back to earlier local traditions and includes as one of its important motifs “bull tied to a kind of post or tree”. The scene greatly resembles the most important iconographic motif of the Indus seals, the “unicorn” bull standing in front of a peculiar stand. Bulls tethered to fig trees are a prominent motif also at Nausharo I D, immediately preceding the Harappan Period Nausharo II. Evidently the roots of the Indus Civilization are in the earlier cultures of the Indo-Iranian borderlands, which in turn are connected with the cultures of the eastern half of the Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia. This wide area remained an interaction sphere even in Harappan times (Lamberg-Karlovsky & Tosi 1973; Cortesi et al. 2008; J.-F. Jarrige et al. 2011), when it was — as in later times — the departure area for new immigrations to the Indus Valley (J.-F. Jarrige & Quivron 2008). The quality of an Indus seal increases with its size, and the largest and most expensive seals _ must have belonged to important persons or institutions. Since the seals were probably worn in a - visible fashion by their owners, as is suggested by the cord holes, they are likely to have second_ arily functioned as indicators of the wearers’ rank, seen at a distance by the size of the seal.73 A few Indus seals are carved hollow and provided with a lid so that something — most probably a magic charm — could be kept inside. This has generally been taken to support the old - hypothesis that the seals, besides their primary function as administrative instruments, also served as protective amulets. In addition to the script, the majority of the Indus seals contain iconographic motifs, whose clearly religious nature has suggested an amuletic function. The pictorial motifs not only rank among the very best preserved examples of Harappan artistic expressions but also provide some of the most important clues to the Harappan religion and to the accompanying inscriptions. The 2nd criterion: the provenance of the objects; and their numbering system It is clearly undesirable to lose control over the sitewise distribution of the objects; a purely typological arrangement mixing objects from all sites would be inadvisable. The site from which the object comes has to be a primary parameter of the classification. Now that seals and inscriptions coming from one and the same site will be distributed in several volumes, a flexible new numbering system is required which will both allow additions at will and make it easy to place the object in its proper context.71 The Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions employs a separate consecutive numbering for each site, prefixed by a letter code which is more easily remembered than a numerical code. The major sites have a short, one-letter code. These sites are, moreover, arranged in each volume according to the total number of seals and inscriptions found at them, in the descending order. The sites which are "smaller" (in respect to the number of seals and inscriptions found at them) have a two-, three- or four-lettered code corresponding to their standard archaeological abbreviations and they are arranged in alphabetical order for easy reference. (See the table of contents.) The letter prefix for the site is followed by a dash and the number of the object assigned to it by its place within the classification sequence. Thus the objects from Mohenjo-daro in this first volume are numbered M-1 to M-620, and they are followed by the objects from Harappa starting with H-1. The objects from Mohenjo-daro in the second volume will start with M-621. Any number of additions can be made. This does not, however, directly imply a chronological correlation between Amri IIC and the BMAC, or Gonur 2.*° In fact, the cultural and chronological position and interplay of the sites in northern Balochistan is still not very well understood since dating features are neither clearly defined nor accurately dated and since regional and/or functional differences may also play a role. We can only briefly add here that a trumpet shaped grey ware vessel was also found in a Sohr Damb III context. According to a series of radiocarbon dates and the stratigraphy, the date of this period cannot be later than 2400 BC. But there are many other features that raise questions as to their date and implications for the wider chronological and cultural constellation. Indus seals and the external contacts of the Indus Civilization Immediately after the first news about the discovery of the Indus Civilization was published in 1924, it became apparent that the Harappans had been in contact with the ancient Western Asiatic cultures. Evidence for this was Indus seals coming from Susa, Ur, and other Mesopotamian sites; among these were both square stamp seals of a purely native Harappan type and seals combining Harappan and local elements such as the cylinder form. Later, a few round Indus seals (a type rarely found in the Indus Valley) were discovered along with a large number of local round stamp seals on the islands of Failaka and Bahrain in the Gulf, where excavations since the 1950's have revealed a flourishing "Dilmun Civilization". Massimo Vidale and Alessandra Lazzari, who participated in the excavations of Shahr-i Sokhta and are in charge of the excavation archives, immediately agreed to my proposal to collect the published glyptic material from Shahr-i Sokhta and include it in this volume. Period I at Shahr-i Sokhta, dated to the early third millennium BCE, witnesses the presence of Proto-Elamites at the site, using Mesopotamian-type cylinder seals, while the local ceramics are related to the Damb-Sadaat/Quetta Ware distributed right to the borders of the Indus Valley. Shahr-i Sokhta was the easternmost point of the Uruk Expansion until Roland Besenval (2011: 49-51 & 133, figs. 121-122) brought to light typically Proto-Elamite bevel-rimmed vessels at Mir-i Qalat in Pakistani Baluchistan. The cylinder seals disappear after Period I, and Period II at Shahr-i Sokhta starts with the introduction of stone and metal seals and related ceramics, apparently coming from southern Turkmenistan (Geoksyur I / Namazga III). This has generally been taken to support the old hypothesis that the seals, besides their primary function as administrative instruments, also served as protective amulets. In addition to the script, the majority of the Indus seals contain iconographic motifs, whose clearly religious nature has suggested an amuletic function. The pictorial motifs not only rank among the very best preserved examples of Harappan artistic expressions but also provide some of the most important clues to the Harappan religion and to the accompanying inscriptions. In addition to being found on the seals, iconographic motifs are found in particular on "tablets". An important general characteristic of this category of objects is that they comprise many identical duplicates. The incised "miniature tablets" from the lower levels of Harappa are the earliest known examples of the fully developed Indus script.3! Later, incised tablets give way to embossed ones, often massproduced in moulds. Sometimes great numbers of similar tablets (especially H-252 ff.) have been found together, or their find places are very close to each other. This has suggested that most of the tablets, both the embossed and the engraved ones, may have functioned as tokens of votive offerings or of visits to temples.32 The inscriptions of the tablets point to such a conclusion, too. The Harappans had a unique script of their own, and thousands of short inscriptions have survived, but the script vanished when the Indus Civilization collapsed. So far there is no such key as the Rosetta Stone, which opened up the secrets of the hieroglyphic writing. This does not mean that it is impossible to gain some understanding of the Indus script, but this demands proper research methods. More than half of the Indus texts have been carved on small stone seals, which usually have some iconographic motif in addition to the text. Normally an animal is depicted very realistically, but there are also for instance anthropomorphic figures probably representing divinities. Indeed, these small seals are our principal sources of Harappan art and religion. The find places of the seals, their material and methods of manufacture, also contribute to the knowledge about Harappan administration, trade routes and crafts. Incised or painted graffiti, including singly occurring “potter’s marks”, form another major inscriptional category. The Kulli culture also retained its separate identity in southern Baluchistan until 1900 BCE. The animal iconography of the Kulli pots goes back to earlier local traditions and includes as one of its important motifs “bull tied to a kind of post or tree”. Bulls tethered to fig trees are a prominent motif also at Nausharo I D, immediately preceding the Harappan Period Nausharo II. Evidently the roots of the Indus Civilization are in the earlier cultures of the Indo-Iranian borderlands, which in turn are connected with the cultures of the eastern half of the Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia. The Indus seals and the discovery of the Indus Civilization The Indus Civilization ranks among the most ancient urban cultures of mankind. It covered an appreciably larger area than either the Early Dynastic Egypt or Sumer. Like the other Old World civilizations, the Indus Civilization seems to have grown from the skilful utilization of the fertile river valleys. Its distinctive characteristics - the gridiron layout of the cities, their elaborate drainage, and the puzzling pictographic script - are still best known from the excavations of Harappa and Mohenjodaro.! Three distinctive seals - representing the object type that has remained most characteristic of the Indus civilization - were found at Harappa in the Punjab and published in 1875, 1886 and 1912.2 But the full implication of these finds was not realized before excavations were started in 1920 at Harappa, and, by chance almost simultaneously, in 1922, at Mohenjo-daro in Sind, some 600 km south in the Indus valley. More seals of the same type were immediately found at both of these sites, and it became evident that an entirely unknown bronze-age civilization had come to light.3 This led to large-scale excavations at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa,* followed by much more limited digs at Chanhujo-daro further south in Sind.5 The bulk of the Indus (or Harappan) seals and inscriptions available to research comes from these excavations in the 1920's and 1930's. In the partition of British India in 1947, all the major sites of the Indus civilization known at that time became part of Pakistan. The language underlying the Indus script has been supposed to be Sumerian, Proto-Dravidian, Proto-Indo-European, Proto-Indo-Iranian, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and so on.40 But no unanimity has been reached even on the basic issues, and most literature on the Indus script requires a lot of sifting in order to pick up useful ideas. The main reason for this unfortunate state of affairs is the fact that all keys that opened other unknown scripts are unavailable here. There are no bi- or multilingual inscriptions giving the same text in both Indus script and some readable characters. There are no understood historical texts which could tell the names of the Harappan gods, kings or cities, or which would quote samples of the language spoken by the Indus people. Even the type of the writing system represented by the Indus script is debated. Moreover, all the texts are short and limited in nature: the average length is five signs, and the longest texts, two identical three-sided tablets (M-494 and M-495), contain 26 signs each. The longest inscription on any single side of an object is found on a seal (M-314) with 17 signs divided into three lines. But students of the Indus script must face these formidable difficulties and the pessimistic prognoses based on them. In fact, some more objective work has been done also. There has been serious discussion of the methodology, and essential research tools in the form of documentation and concordances have been created. On one point, at least, most scholars agree: the direction of writing usually is from right to left (but in the seal stamps, engraved in mirror image, from left to right); however, in some texts (particularly in the early tablets from Harappa) the direction of writing runs from left to right, and in a few texts alternatingly, boustrophedon.4! We cannot enter into a detailed discussion of the Indus script and its study here. Various comparisons have been made with the ancient West Asian glyptics as well as with the later art of classical India.35 Although it is impossible to go into detail here, one further example may be briefly mentioned because of its intrinsic interest and also in order to point out that these two kinds of comparisons need not be mutually exclusive. Sir John Marshall's identification of a "ProtoSiva" in the buffalo-horned deity of a famous seal from Mohenjo-daro (M-304)36 may well be correct, and so may be Alf Hiltebeitel's even more convincing identification of this figure as "ProtoMahisa"37, although this deity and his “yogic posture" have close counterparts in the earlier glyptic art of the Proto-Elamites.78 Comparative studies thus suggest that the Indus Civilization may have been an integral if marginal part of the West Asian cultural area and that there is an unbroken cultural continuity in South Asia from the Harappan times until the present day. 4. chunk_text: order to understand better the formation process of the Indus Civilization and the background of its seals, including foreign seals found in Harappan contexts, it seems necessary to widen the scope of CISI to include also seals discovered in archaeological excavations of prehistoric eastern Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia (excluding the great multitude of seals that come from looted graves of these regions). An important site, with seals closely related to those of Mundigak and Mehrgarh, is Shahr-i Sokhta, the capital of the “Helmand Civilization” of ancient Seistan. Massimo Vidale and Alessandra Lazzari, who participated in the excavations of Shahr-i Sokhta and are in charge of the excavation archives, immediately agreed to my proposal to collect the published glyptic material from Shahr-i Sokhta and include it in this volume. They also wrote an introductory essay and sent me relevant publications not accessible in Helsinki. Period I at Shahr-i Sokhta, dated to the early third millennium BCE, witnesses the presence of Proto-Elamites at the site, using Mesopotamian-type cylinder seals, while the local ceramics are related to the Damb-Sadaat/Quetta Ware distributed right to the borders of the Indus Valley. Shahr-i Sokhta was the easternmost point of the Uruk Expansion until Roland Besenval (2011: 49-51 & 133, figs. 121-122) brought to light typically Proto-Elamite bevel-rimmed vessels at Mir-i Qalat in Pakistani Baluchistan. The cylinder seals disappear after Period I, and Period II at Shahr-i Sokhta starts with the introduction of stone and metal seals and related ceramics, apparently coming from southern Turkmenistan (Geoksyur I / Namazga III). As many seals and sealings from Shahr-i Sokhta have not been assigned to definite periods, the material has been arranged typologically. The site of Chanhu-daro, in lower Sindh, was excavated by Ernest Mackay in 1935-36 (CE, 1943). Most of the finds remained in India, and the seals from Chanhu-daro in the care of the ASI were published in CISI 1. Many seals and other objects, however, could be taken to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (BMFA), which had been financing the excavation. These seals from Chanhu-daro are published in this volume with the excellent photographs provided by the BMFA. The Kulli culture also retained its separate identity in southern Baluchistan until 1900 BCE. The animal iconography of the Kulli pots goes back to earlier local traditions and includes as one of its important motifs “bull tied to a kind of post or tree”. The scene greatly resembles the most important iconographic motif of the Indus seals, the “unicorn” bull standing in front of a peculiar stand. Bulls tethered to fig trees are a prominent motif also at Nausharo I D, immediately preceding the Harappan Period Nausharo II. Evidently the roots of the Indus Civilization are in the earlier cultures of the Indo-Iranian borderlands, which in turn are connected with the cultures of the eastern half of the Iranian Plateau and southern Central Asia. This wide area remained an interaction sphere even in Harappan times (Lamberg-Karlovsky & Tosi 1973; Cortesi et al. 2008; J.-F. Significance of the Symbols: New Elements Furnished by the Excavated Sites Among the different possible interpretations, the marks are sometimes described as representing goods which might be contained in the vessels or indicated their capacity. A number of Mesopotamian pots bear inscriptions indicating their capacity, particularly the large jars. At Mehrgarh, the great majority of incised pots are small goblets and plates which are not shape types of vessels made to conserve goods. As for the capacity, 21 different sign types have been recorded on the side or underside of bases of hundreds of almost identical goblets and in many other cases, the same symbol was incised on vessels of different shapes and sizes. It is also difficult sometimes to analyse the incised marks from various sites because many of them were found on potsherds or on vessels not always assigned to particular periods or areas. This is not the case at Mehrgarh and Nausharo where numerous groups of complete incised pots were found in structures linked to potter’s workshops. A dense accumulation of jars mostly identical in form was uncovered in the levels of Period VI. This structure is an open firing of superimposed layers of clay jars in which the bulk of the vessels was abandoned due to a failure of the firing process (Audouze & Jarrige 1979). Many jars in this structure were used as firing containers or saggars in a phase of the manufacturing cycle. A semifluid mixture of clay and straw covered the external surface of their rims, probably to stick a lid on, and one of them was even entirely covered with this coat of clay. The purpose of these jars was to protect objects or vases from breakage as well as from combustion gas and flames in a reducing atmosphere. This technique, known at Mehrgarh at the end of the fourth millennium, was also used later at Mohenjo-daro where a group of coated jars was uncovered. The mouth of one of them was sealed with the classic unicorn seal. This continuity of use of pre-firing marks, although much less frequently, seems to argue against the hypothesis that the roots of the Indus script are in the incised marks tradition of some predecessors. The simple designs of the comparable pre-existing signs, easily produced by a tool or a stylus, may be the reason why they were adopted, intentionally or not, in the Indus script. MEADOW Introduction Ever since the discovery of the first engraved seals of the Indus Civilization at the site of Harappa, scholars have been trying to unlock the secrets of the Indus script’ and to understand the social, economic, and political importance of these and other inscribed objects. Although the inscriptions have remained undeciphered, it has been possible to gain some insight into the context for the use of the script based on carefully documented recovery of inscribed objects from recent excavations throughout the greater Indus region. In this volume, we present for the first time in one place the assemblage of inscribed and incised objects discovered at the site of Harappa during excavations conducted between 1986-2007 by the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (HARP)’. ' That “writing” and “script” are appropriate terms to employ in reference to what has commonly been called the “Indus script” has been contested by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004). They argue that the Indus script is not likely to have been linked directly to a spoken language and was probably a system of non-linguistic symbols. We, however, contend that given the development in the system of inscriptions over time as seen at Harappa and given the extensive use of the “signs” or “symbols” both formally and informally and on many media (see text discussion), making the distinction between a language-based script and a not-so-tied-to-language symboling system is not a particularly interesting distinction. In any event, in the absence of multi-lingual texts, long texts, and/or a successor symboling system or script, there can be no widely accepted understanding of what the symbols or signs of the “Indus script” actually meant to those who employed them, and thus there can be no true resolution of this issue. As a result, we continue to employ terms like “script” and even “writing” in their broadest senses and are well aware that not everyone may agree with such usage. We are also rather imprecise in our use of the terms “inscribed” and “inscription”, which we employ broadly in relation to the Indus script and not in the restricted sense of something engraved, incised, or written. Thus pieces with script in relief are also referred to as inscribed (although not “incised”).
