Incised and Painted Marks on the Pottery of Mehrgarh and Nausharo-Baluchistan XXV Many symbols are common to the various sites.2 But this visible similarity of signs is most probably due to the use, in each corpus, of a range of simple geometric designs which are also comparable with many symbols occurring in elaborate writing systems. Many signs have parallels in the proto-Elamite script ( fig. 1, sign no. 82 and fig. 2, signs no. 20, 21, 22, 28, 34, A1, 43 and 45) as well as with many basic signs of the Indus script (Parpola 1994). The relationship between the two writing systems has often been suggested by the possibility of a link through the pre-Indus incised marks on pottery (Potts 1981).2 But many comparable marks from Susiana or Mehrgarh IV are dated earlier than the creation of the proto-Elamite system and similar pre-firing marks were still incised on vessels at a time when the Indus script was already known. This continuity of use of pre-firing marks, although much less frequently, seems to argue against the hypothesis that the roots of the Indus script are in the incised marks tradition of some predecessors. The simple designs of the comparable pre-existing signs, easily produced by a tool or a stylus, may be the reason why they were adopted, intentionally or not, in the Indus script. The pre-firing marks are always single signs and the assumption that they may have been part or variants of even a crude form of writing cannot be proved, but they probably represent a system of mutually intelligible symbols commonly accepted through time and space, and it seems likely that these incised marks were merely utilitarian. chunk_text: Preface The roots of this volume go back to 1964, when three young Finns decided to study the undeciphered Indus script with the help of the computer. Seppo Koskenniemi worked as a scientific adviser for IBM, Simo Parpola studied Assyriology, and Asko Parpola studied Indology. We had about 2200 Indus texts at our disposal in photographs and drawings, almost all of them published in the reports of the archaeological excavations that had been carried out at Harappa (EH), Mohenjo-daro (MIC, FEM) and Chanhu-daro (Mackay 1943). While transcribing these pictographic texts into code numbers for computer processing, we became aware of some limitations in our sources. Details are not always clear in the natural size photographs of inscribed objects, which mostly are rather small; some photographs are out of focus or not well exposed; and one could not be sure of the reliability of the drawings. In 1971, I visited the principal museums in Pakistan and India in order to check the accuracy of our readings of the Indus texts from the originals. To my surprise, the museum collections contained some 400 Indus seals and other inscribed objects from Harappa and Mohenjodaro that had not been published in the excavation reports. It turned out that these objects came from excavations that had been carried out after the reported official digs. Photographs of some of the objects excavated by the curators of the site museums of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were published in the Annual Reports of the Archaeological Survey of India, but mostly these reports were brief and without illustrations, and so there was no detailed record of this material. It was clear that the objects thus newly discovered in the museums had to be properly published. Taking into consideration the drawbacks of the then existing publications, I started negotiating with the Archaeological Survey of India, the Department of Archaeology and Museums, Government of Pakistan, and the Finnish Academy of Sciences and Letters about a collaborative project aiming to bring out a comprehensive publication that would make all the material available in as good photographs as possible. The language underlying the Indus script has been supposed to be Sumerian, Proto-Dravidian, Proto-Indo-European, Proto-Indo-Iranian, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and so on.40 But no unanimity has been reached even on the basic issues, and most literature on the Indus script requires a lot of sifting in order to pick up useful ideas. The main reason for this unfortunate state of affairs is the fact that all keys that opened other unknown scripts are unavailable here. There are no bi- or multilingual inscriptions giving the same text in both Indus script and some readable characters. There are no understood historical texts which could tell the names of the Harappan gods, kings or cities, or which would quote samples of the language spoken by the Indus people. Even the type of the writing system represented by the Indus script is debated. Moreover, all the texts are short and limited in nature: the average length is five signs, and the longest texts, two identical three-sided tablets (M-494 and M-495), contain 26 signs each. The longest inscription on any single side of an object is found on a seal (M-314) with 17 signs divided into three lines. But students of the Indus script must face these formidable difficulties and the pessimistic prognoses based on them. In fact, some more objective work has been done also. There has been serious discussion of the methodology, and essential research tools in the form of documentation and concordances have been created. chunk_text: Authority Structure and the Evolution of Early Writing Systems Reclassifying the Indus Script Through Comparative Administrative Typology Abstract The Indus script has long been treated as an anomalous or incomplete writing system due to its short inscriptions, lack of phonetic decipherment, and apparent disappearance without textual descendants. This paper proposes a reclassification of the Indus script as a fully realized nonphonetic administrative operator system, optimized for governance within a distributed trade network rather than a centralized state. By identifying a shared semantic operator grammar across the Indus script, early Mesopotamian cuneiform, and early Chinese writing, and by testing this grammar against control cases from Shang oracle bone inscriptions and early Mesopotamian administrative tablets, this study demonstrates that divergence in script evolution correlates with authority topology, not cognitive or cultural capacity. The Indus script is shown to terminate at a point of functional sufficiency aligned with network authority, rather than failing to evolve toward language. 1. The Problem of the Indus Script Despite more than a century of study, the Indus script remains undeciphered in phonetic terms. Its inscriptions are short, highly repetitive, and largely confined to seals and a small number of public signboards. Traditional expectations that writing systems evolve toward phonetic representation, narrative expression, and historical memory have led to the Indus script being framed as primitive, incomplete, or interrupted by civilizational collapse. This framing assumes that linguistic encoding is the natural endpoint of writing. However, comparative evidence from other early writing systems suggests that writing initially emerges not as language, but as administrative technology. This paper argues that the Indus script should be evaluated according to the functional demands of its authority structure rather than by comparison to later literary traditions. 2. Results reveal these to have been dynamic periods of urban expansion together with recurrent decay, rebuilding, and reorganization in different parts of the city. In 2000 and 2001, excavations turned to recovering more information on Period 3A in order to reveal initial Harappa Phase developments, particularly relating to the use of inscribed pieces. This period is poorly represented in excavations at most Indus sites, because the remains are buried under later occupation levels. At Harappa, it has been possible to recover two seal fragments from Period 3A, providing an important baseline against which to evaluate stylistic and technological change in the use of seals (see below for more discussion). Based on evidence at hand to date, square seals with script together with the unicorn or other animal motifs are associated primarily with the Tater part of Period 3A and are relatively common throughout Period 3B and on into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997). Square seals with script alone are found first in Period 3B, but long rectangular seals with script alone are confined to Period 3C. We are also obtaining important chronological information with respect to inscribed tablets, which are particularly common at Harappa, more so than the seals. Through careful stratigraphic cutting-back of Vats’ section in Trench I of Mound F and comparison with his report of that trench (Vats 1940), we have determined that he was not correct in reporting that small steatite tablets with incised script are from the earliest levels of the site. Instead it is evident that such tablets appeared toward the middle of Period 3B and continued to be used well into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). Furthermore, these inscribed steatite tablets, which Vats (1940) called “tiny steatite seals”, are not seals at all but are incised with script that was to be read directly from the tablet. And along with the steatite tablets are found terracotta and glazed faience tablets with molded bas-relief script, motifs, and narrative scenes, which also start appearing in mid-Period 3B and continue into Period 3C (Meadow & Kenoyer 1997; 2000). The purpose and scope of the Corpus The texts in standardized editions and corcordances are based upon the subjective judgements of individual scholars, and they do not display all the intricacies of the originals. Moreover, they contain numerous admittedly doubtful readings. Objective photographic documentation of the original inscriptions thus is a necessary complement to such textual studies. Photographs of the original objects are equally indispensable tools for the historians of art and religion studying the iconographic motifs and for archaeologists engaged in a comparative study of the objects. In short, there is no replacement for good photographs of all the Indus seals and inscriptions. A major part of the material has been published in photographs in the excavation reports of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa: they illustrate altogether roughly 2500 objects. These publications have long been out of print and difficult to procure. It is true that they have been reprinted in recent years, but the quality of the photographs in the reprints is so low that they are practically unusable. The published photographs of the rest of the material, on the other hand, are scattered in a number of publications, and their mere collection involves great difficulties for persons without access to specialized libraries. It would have been simple enough to collect and reproduce the old photographs of the earlier publications. Such a procedure, however, would have resulted in a book that would not have fully satisfied the serious student of the Indus script and iconography. Harappa Phase Carved Seals Only two seals, both incomplete, have been recovered from the lowest levels of the Harappa Phase (Period 3A). One example (H-1688) is a broken steatite seal from street deposits on Mound E, dating to ca. 2600 BC. (Kenoyer 1991; Dales, Kenoyer et al. 1991, fig. 13.44e). The style of carving is bold and angular, consisting of a single sign above the rump of a bovine, which, to judge by comparison with a complete seal from the site of Farmana in Haryana, might be a water buffalo (Shinde et al. 2008: 104, fig. 107). The deeply carved V-shaped sign or symbol has not been found on any later seal, but a rounder and more symmetrical form does occur on molded tablets. The animals carved on later seals also are more naturalistic with smooth contours that reflect the actual muscles of the animal. The second Period 3A seal fragment from Harappa (H-1689) comes from a deposit on the western edge of Mound E that was found to contain both Early Harappan and Harappan pottery. This seal has an elephant motif with naturalistic lines and may represent the development of seal carving styles at the end of Period 3A or the beginning of Period 3B. Further welldated examples are needed to clarify the earliest style of seal carving, but these two seal fragments from Harappa, and the examples from Farmana, suggest that styles of carving seals evolved over time and that some of the signs also changed over time.

A note on the material and production of the objects and on the colour photographs Space forbids discussing the material and production of the Indus seals and inscriptions in any detail here; for this the reader is once again referred to the excavation reports. It can only be noted that the great majority of the Indus seals are made of steatite, generally whitish in colour. The seals were first sawed and cut into their forms and then polished; the subject was outlined with a sharp point and then engraved with a drill. Finally the seal was coated with an alkali and heated. It seems that the alkali coating was applied mainly to dark steatite in order to make it white. Heating hardens the steatite, which is a very soft stone, and thus protects it against wear. The various stages of this process can been seen from different examples, the unfinished ones being particularly instructive.85 The moulded tablets are normally made of terracotta or faience, but there are also a few cast copper tablets (placed at the end), while the incised tablets usually are of steatite or copper. chunk_text: Seals and Sealings from the Ahar-Banas Culture MARTA AMERI The sites that belong to the Ahar-Banas complex are located primarily in the Mewar region of southwestern Rajasthan, to the east of the Aravalli mountain range, which runs from Gujarat to Delhi and bisects the state diagonally. They cluster around the Banas River and its tributaries, the Ahar, the Berach, the Gambiri, the Kothari and the Khari.' The sites vary in size from a tiny 0.3 hectares (Tarawat) to a fairly substantial 22 ha. (Gilund), but seem to cluster at around five hectares in size. The exploration of the Ahar-Banas Culture began with the excavations at the site of Ahar, in Rajasthan, in 1952, and then again in 1954—55 and 1955-56. These excavations exposed a copper-using, agriculturally-based culture that was defined by a White Painted Black and Red Ware pottery but showed little connection to the Harappan sites found further to the south and west. Surveys conducted in this part of southeastern Rajasthan revealed almost 50 more sites with the typical White Painted Black and Red Ware and a similar subsistence base (Misra 1967: 148). In 1959, Gilund, a second site belonging to the same cultural milieu as Ahar was excavated by B. B. Lal (Ghosh 1960). Excavations at Ahar were eventually resumed by H. D Sankalia in 1962. Most of the sites excavated and surveyed were briefly published in Indian Archaeology — A Review’, but only Ahar was fully published by Sankalia in 1969 (Sankalia et al. 1969). The material from these two sites, Ahar and Gilund, though originally loosely defined and poorly published, served as the basis for the exploration and definition of the AharBanas cultural complex until the 1990s when Deccan College opened up its field school at Balathal (Hooja 1988). Renewed excavations at Gilund in the early 2000s? and the exploration of new sites at Chatrikhera (Raczek et al. 2010) and Pachamta (Raczek et al. 2019) have served to further expand our knowledge of this area. The Chalcolithic period in the Ahar-Banas is generally divided into three phases based on archaeological materials and radiocarbon dates from various sites. chunk_text: the International Conference on Karakorum Culture, organized by Professor Ahmad Hasan Dani in Gilgit. He wanted to check if any Indus inscriptions were to be found among the petroglyphs newly discovered in large quantities by the joint German-Pakistani research team led by Professor Karl Jettmar and Professor Dani. While this inquiry regrettably yielded negative results, the conference gave Dr Parpola an opportunity to discuss the CISI project with Dr M. Ishtiaq Khan and with Dr M. Rafique Mughal, both of whom participated in the conference. After his return from Bahrain, Dr Mughal had been appointed Director of the Northern Circle of the DAMGP based in Lahore. Dr Parpola proposed to send a Finnish photographer to complete the remaining documentation.
